candidate.answerReason: Equal pair weights require either four genuine coins or one counterfeit in each pair. These cases have 420 and 112 equally likely ordered pair selections, respectively, so the conditional probability is 420/532 = 15/19.

methods.label: Count the possible pair selections
methods.explanation:
The weight information tells us which selections remain possible. Let \(g\) be a genuine coin's weight and \(f\ne g\) a counterfeit coin's weight. A pair containing \(k\) counterfeit coins weighs
\[
2g+k(f-g).
\]
Because \(f-g\ne0\), two pairs have equal weight exactly when they contain the same number of counterfeit coins. There are only two counterfeits altogether, so the equal-weight cases are four genuine coins, or one counterfeit in each pair.

Treat the coins as individually distinguishable for counting. Every choice of a first unordered pair followed by a second unordered pair has the same probability: there are always \(\binom{10}{2}\) choices first and \(\binom82\) choices second.

For four genuine coins, choose the first pair from the eight genuine coins and the second from the six genuine coins left:
\[
\binom82\binom62=28\cdot15=420.
\]
For one counterfeit in each pair, the first pair has \(2\cdot8\) choices. After that, the second pair has \(1\cdot7\) choices:
\[
(2\cdot8)(1\cdot7)=112.
\]
The two cases are disjoint and exhaust all equal-weight selections. Each selection is counted once because the first and second pairs are distinguished, while order within a pair is ignored. Restricting to these equal-weight outcomes gives
\[
\frac{420}{420+112}=\boxed{\frac{15}{19}},
\]
which is choice D.
methods.levelReason: This is elementary conditional probability computed by combinations and two exhaustive cases.

methods.label: Multiply the drawing probabilities
methods.explanation:
Let \(g\) and \(f\ne g\) be the genuine and counterfeit weights. A pair with \(k\) counterfeits weighs \(2g+k(f-g)\), so equal pair weights require equal counterfeit counts. With only two counterfeits available, either all four selected coins are genuine or each pair contains one counterfeit.

Imagine drawing the coins one at a time, with the first two forming the first pair. The probability that all four are genuine is
\[
p=\frac8{10}\cdot\frac79\cdot\frac68\cdot\frac57
=\frac13.
\]
The denominators and numerators decrease because no coins are replaced.

For the other equal-weight case, the first pair can be counterfeit–genuine or genuine–counterfeit. These disjoint orders have equal probability, so the probability of a mixed first pair is
\[
2\cdot\frac2{10}\cdot\frac89=\frac{16}{45}.
\]
After such a pair, one counterfeit and seven genuine coins remain. The probability that the second pair is also mixed is
\[
2\cdot\frac18\cdot\frac77=\frac14.
\]
Thus the probability of one counterfeit in each pair is
\[
q=\frac{16}{45}\cdot\frac14=\frac4{45}.
\]
The two equal-weight cases are disjoint, so their total probability is \(p+q=19/45>0\). Given that the weights are equal, the desired probability is
\[
\frac{p}{p+q}
=\frac{1/3}{19/45}
=\boxed{\frac{15}{19}},
\]
which is choice D.
methods.levelReason: Sequential fractions provide a complete AMC 10 route without combination formulas or distribution theory.

candidate.annotationRationale: The central target is conditional probability after learning that the pair weights agree. Both methods identify the conditioning event and respect sampling without replacement. The counting route uses equally likely pair selections and combinations; the sequential route instead uses conditional multiplication and addition of disjoint probabilities. Those alternative techniques are method-local.

review.mathematicalCheck: A pair with k counterfeits weighs 2g+k(f-g), so equal weights require equal counterfeit counts. The exhaustive cases have 420 and 112 equally likely pair selections, giving 420/532 = 15/19. The sequential method independently obtains probabilities 1/3 and 4/45 and the same conditional ratio.
